content: Emtricitabine is a synthetic nucleoside analog of cytidine. Once inside the cell, it undergoes phosphorylation by cellular enzymes to form emtricitabine 5'-triphosphate. This active metabolite inhibits the activity of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate, deoxycytidine 5'-triphosphate, and by being incorporated into the growing viral DNA chain, leading to chain termination. Emtricitabine 5'-triphosphate exhibits minimal inhibitory effects on mammalian DNA polymerases α, β, ε, and mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ. The antiviral activity of emtricitabine has been studied in cell culture against both laboratory and clinical isolates of HIV-1. These studies utilized lymphoblastoid cell lines, the MAGI-CCR5 cell line, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The 50% effective concentration (EC50) of emtricitabine ranged from 0.0013 to 0.64 µM (0.0003–0.158 µg/mL). Combination studies with other antiretroviral agents, including nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), and protease inhibitors, demonstrated additive to synergistic effects. Emtricitabine also showed antiviral activity against various HIV-1 clades (A, B, C, D, E, F, and G) with EC50 values ranging from 0.007 to 0.075 µM and exhibited strain-specific activity against HIV-2, with EC50 values ranging from 0.007 to 1.5 µM. Clinical trials involving 101 subjects who received 25–400 mg of emtricitabine daily as monotherapy for 10–14 days demonstrated a dose-dependent antiviral effect. A median reduction in plasma HIV-1 RNA of 1.3 log10 was observed at a dose of 25 mg once daily, while reductions of 1.7 log10 to 1.9 log10 were seen at doses of 200 mg once or twice daily. Resistance to emtricitabine has been observed both in vitro and in vivo. Genotypic analysis of resistant HIV-1 isolates revealed that reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine was associated with a mutation at codon 184 of the reverse transcriptase gene, resulting in the substitution of methionine with valine or isoleucine (M184V/I). In clinical trials, emtricitabine-resistant isolates were identified in subjects treated with emtricitabine alone or in combination with other antiretroviral agents. For example, in a study involving treatment-naive subjects receiving emtricitabine, didanosine, and efavirenz, 37.5% of subjects with virologic failure had viral isolates with reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine due to the M184V/I mutation. In another trial comparing emtricitabine, tenofovir, and efavirenz with zidovudine/lamivudine and efavirenz, resistance analysis at Week 144 revealed that the M184V mutation occurred in 2 out of 19 subjects in the emtricitabine/tenofovir group and in 10 out of 29 subjects in the lamivudine/zidovudine group. Notably, no subjects in the emtricitabine/tenofovir group developed the K65R mutation, which is associated with resistance to multiple NRTIs. Cross-resistance among certain nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors has been documented. HIV-1 isolates with the M184V/I mutation, which confers resistance to emtricitabine, also exhibit cross-resistance to lamivudine and zalcitabine. However, these isolates remain sensitive to didanosine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine, and NNRTIs such as delavirdine, efavirenz, and nevirapine. HIV-1 isolates with the K65R mutation, which is selected in vivo by drugs like abacavir, didanosine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine, show reduced susceptibility to emtricitabine. Conversely, viruses with mutations conferring resistance to stavudine and zidovudine (e.g., M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y/F, K219Q/E) or to didanosine (e.g., L74V) remain susceptible to emtricitabine. Additionally, HIV-1 isolates with the K103N mutation, which is associated with resistance to NNRTIs, retain susceptibility to emtricitabine.
